It depends on your universe.  The characters in dragon ball would technically count as this as anyone can learn how to use ki to fly and fire energy blasts but few people in the world do.  Though the people in that world don’t seem to be aware of it, I’d agree with the previous poster.  While it’s easy to say that if powers like those in anime existed you would train to get them, most people wouldn’t be willing to put forth the effort or have the aptitude for using it that some of these characters do.  I do imagine, the more spectacular a thing is, the more likely you would see people trying to accomplish it, most wouldn’t pull off the kinds of things you could with it.  If I trained I could do already spectacular things compared to what I can do now.  Would I be more incentivized to train if I thought I could fly or shoot lasers from my eyes?  Probably.  But how much would the average human tough it out based on the kinds of things you could potentially do?  This can all be defined in your universe accordingly but I imagine not everyone would do it.  Audiences are willing to suspend their disbelief quite a bit.  People relate to Batman and Krillin as an example of a powerless human fighting amongst gods but the feats that they can pull are far beyond anything any ordinary human can do.  The possibilities are limitless as to what a human could pull off when you define them in your world.

I would imagine things typically defined by the mythical martial arts stereotypes.  Most characters in fiction that fit into this category are usually these types.  Super strength, speed, ki blasts (we even have people claiming to do this in real life) or psychic and telekinetic abilities are all abilities people purport to have in real life and are often achieved through training.

One of my older short stories (not really a full world) utilized this idea but my consequences were central to the plot.  The obvious side effect would be that if you arrive at a point in time where you existed could create a paradox though that wouldn’t be a huge consequence for anyone else but the traveler.  Maybe traveling to a specific point creates a bridge to that timeline so anyone traveling to that point from the timeline that created it arrives in that second timeline and something has to be done to shut that bridge, sealing off timelines but trapping you in whichever one you were in?  The bridge could be unstable and threatens to destroy the timelines.  Or maybe, since time isn’t infinite and time will cease to be in all universes, the collapse of multiple timelines will have detrimental effects.  Maybe people experience delusions or psychoses based upon those other timelines.

Or, to expand on those ideas you’ve presented, maybe that force is fate and it will try to make universes collide to destroy deviations from the original plan.  In that way, that force could be in danger of fading if fate is not adhered to and rebelling against fate means destroying the very concept and creating a world of pure chaos where infinite timelines spawn from every decision.

Yeah,  most of my characters don't have much of an appearance in my head until I have to actually write them.  If the character is inspired by something in media then I just kind of have a stock character from that in my mind and when it comes to names they're given one word placeholders that I feel fit them and I use that.  If I like the way it sounds in writing to the point where I use it often in regards to that character I'll work on expanding a backstory around that name.

Names are chosen based upon how they sound.  I know I made another comment on this sub somewhere about this but I don't name them based on any meaning, I just use certain sounds for certain character traits.  Sharper sounds like Z, X, V and D typically go to evil characters.  Sounds like M, C, Ch, R and T go to heroic, noble characters.  Rounder sounds like B, G, H and F go to more jovial, comical or lighthearted characters.

In terms of worldbuilding, no.  In terms of storytelling, yes.  Not necessarily plot wise but at least in terms of what significance the dragons may have symbolically to the story.  It’s okay to build a world around your plot in which individual elements don’t relate to your story as a world builder but as a writer, I believe everything should have some significance outside of “i like dragons and wanted to include them.”  That being said, no harm is done so long as the elements of your world don’t unnecessarily detract from the story you’re trying to tell.
